summary: Students (ages 13–14) learn the engineering of deep-ocean exploration as a set of trade-offs forced by a harsh, quantifiable environment: pressure rising ~1 atm per 10 m, near-freezing cold, total darkness, and the fact that seawater strongly absorbs radio waves, so radio works only over very short distances (sound/sonar and tethers are used instead; visible light also fades within tens of metres, which is why craft carry their own lights). They distinguish 'mapped' (broad, coarse sonar) from 'seen/observed' (tiny camera footprint), compare tool classes (crewed submersibles such as Alvin and Deepsea Challenger, ROVs, AUVs, and multibeam sonar) on cost/depth/endurance/data/risk, and reason about why roughly a quarter of the seafloor is mapped at high resolution while only about 0.001% or less of the deep seafloor has been directly observed. A mission-planning simulation is the central activity; a labelled cutaway, an in-role pilot conversation, an ROV-piloting spatial task, and a consolidation quiz support and extend it.
misconceptions: 'We've explored most of the ocean' — only ~a quarter is mapped at high resolution and far less than 1% (<0.001% of deep seafloor) has been directly observed.
'Mapping the seafloor means we've seen it' — sonar gives shape/depth, not imagery; 'mapped' and 'seen' are very different coverage.
'Radio works underwater like it does in air' — seawater blocks radio/EM, so deep vehicles rely on sound (sonar/acoustic comms) and tethers.
'Submarines can just go to the bottom of any trench' — pressure at full-ocean depth is over 1,000 atm; only specially engineered craft survive it.
'We know less about the ocean than the Moon' (as a blanket fact) — an outdated slogan; the accurate claim is about high-resolution mapping and direct observation, not knowledge in general.

activities.title: Mission control: descend, survive the pressure, and cover the seafloor
steps: Choose a vehicle (crewed submersible, ROV, AUV, or surface multibeam sonar) with the goal of exploring the deep seafloor under a cost/time budget.

Send a craft down while watching a live depth/pressure gauge rise about +1 atm every 10 m and a hull-stress indicator climb; if a thin hull is sent too deep it implodes, so re-spec a thicker pressure sphere and note the resulting rise in weight and cost.
When radio communication drops out underwater, switch the comms panel to sonar/acoustic links or a physical tether.

Switch to a coverage map: spend a dive and watch a crewed sub or ROV light only a pinprick footprint of the seafloor grid, then turn on the ship's multibeam sonar and watch it paint broad but coarse swaths.

Race budget and time and observe the 'mapped' area creep toward about a quarter of the seafloor while the directly 'seen' area stays an almost invisible sliver (roughly 0.001% or less of the deep seafloor).
Compare tools in a picker/table showing cost, depth reach, endurance, and data return.
activities.insight: Each vehicle earns its place by trading cost, reach, endurance, data and risk; crushing pressure forces heavy pressure spheres and expensive dives; radio fails underwater so sound and tethers are needed; and 'mapped' and 'seen' are very different, which is why so much of the deep sea is mapped coarsely yet almost none is directly observed.

activities.title: Labelled cutaway and depth–pressure column
steps: Examine a submersible/ROV cutaway and identify the pressure sphere, thrusters, manipulator arm, lights, and tether/sonar, noting the function of each.

Read a depth column that marks the operating depths of Alvin, ROVs, AUVs and multibeam sonar against a pressure scale (~1 atm per 10 m), alongside milestone dives such as Trieste and Deepsea Challenger (to Challenger Deep).
Compare a 'mapped' panel (broad, coarse sonar swath) against a 'seen' panel (pinprick camera footprint).
Compute the approximate pressure a craft faces at a stated depth, e.g. ~400 atm at 4,000 m, using ~1 atm per 10 m.
activities.insight: The hardware components are solutions to specific environmental constraints, each tool class works at a characteristic depth range, and mapping coverage is far broader than direct observation coverage.

activities.title: Interview a deep-sea pilot or ocean engineer
steps: Interview an in-role Alvin pilot or ROV engineer about what a dive feels like — the pressure, the darkness, the cold, and how communication works.
Ask why crewed dives happen at all given the cost and risk, and how the team decides where to look.
Raise the 'harder than reaching the Moon in some ways' comparison and the idea of reusing this technology on ocean worlds like Europa and Enceladus, and press for reasons.
activities.insight: Deep-sea exploration involves real human judgement and lived constraints; the Moon comparison is about high-resolution mapping and direct observation, not knowledge in general; and the same engineering ideas are proposed for reuse in astrobiology missions beyond Earth.

activities.title: Pilot an ROV through a dark trench (spatial task)
steps: Fly an ROV through a dark canyon or wreck with only a limited cone of light, managing a tether as you go.
Notice how little of the surroundings you can see at any moment and how the tether constrains movement.
activities.insight: The deep sea is genuinely three-dimensional and dark; direct observation covers only a tiny footprint at a time, which reinforces why 'seen' coverage stays so small.

activities.title: Consolidate the physics and tool taxonomy
steps: Use a slider to read the pressure at a given depth (e.g. 4,000 m) and check it against ~1 atm per 10 m.
Match each tool (Alvin-type crewed sub, ROV, AUV, multibeam sonar) to its role and typical depth.
Sequence the steps of a dive and categorise example coverage as 'mapped' or 'seen'.
Answer why radio fails underwater and what is used instead.
activities.insight: Students can recall and apply the pressure relationship, the tool taxonomy, the comms physics, and the mapped-versus-seen distinction.

checkQuestion: Only about a quarter of the ocean floor has been mapped in high resolution, and reaching the deep sea needs special submersibles and ROVs — even though it's on our own planet and far closer than the Moon. A student says 'that's just because nobody's bothered to go — if we wanted to, a strong submarine and a radio would sort it out quickly'. Is it mainly a lack of effort, and would a tough sub plus a radio really do it? Explain the real obstacles and how the technology gets around them.
checkAnswer: It's not lack of effort — the deep ocean is genuinely one of the hardest places to explore. The obstacles are physical: crushing pressure (hundreds of times surface pressure, needing extremely strong crewed submersibles like Alvin/Deepsea Challenger or uncrewed ROVs), total darkness (must carry powerful lights and cameras), intense cold, and the fact that radio waves DON'T travel through seawater — so communication and positioning rely on acoustics (sonar), and deep vehicles are often tethered or use acoustic links, not radio. Mapping is slow because high-resolution maps need ships criss-crossing with sonar (satellites only give a coarse picture through water), which is why only ~25% is mapped at high resolution. So a 'strong sub and a radio' fails at the first hurdle: the radio won't work and the pressure/darkness/scale still have to be engineered around — the same reasons the deep sea can be harder to reach than the Moon's surface.
